questions.question: How would you describe your organisation's core data storage and platform architecture?
questions.level_1: Data lives in disconnected spreadsheets and local files. No shared platform exists.
questions.level_3: A defined data platform exists (warehouse, lakehouse, or equivalent) with documented ownership and access rules.
questions.level_5: A unified, monitored platform serves all business units, with capacity and performance actively managed against demand.

questions.question: How are data pipelines built and run across your organisation?
questions.level_1: Data is moved manually: exports, email attachments, copy-paste between systems.
questions.level_3: Pipelines are scripted and scheduled, with documented ownership and failure alerts.
questions.level_5: Pipelines are orchestrated, version-controlled, and automatically tested before deployment, with lineage tracked end to end.

questions.question: How do your core systems (CRM, finance, operations) share data with each other?
questions.level_1: Systems do not share data automatically. Integration means someone re-keys or re-uploads.
questions.level_3: Point-to-point integrations exist for the highest-priority systems, documented and maintained.
questions.level_5: Integration runs on a managed API or event-driven layer, with new systems onboarded to a standard pattern, not a one-off build.

questions.question: How would your infrastructure cope with a sudden 5x increase in data volume or user demand?
questions.level_1: It would not. Capacity is fixed and any growth requires manual, reactive intervention.
questions.level_3: Capacity can be increased, but it requires planning and lead time; scaling is not automatic.
questions.level_5: Infrastructure scales elastically against demand, with cost and performance monitored continuously.

questions.question: What happens to your data and systems if a critical platform fails today?
questions.level_1: There is no tested backup or recovery plan. Recovery time and data loss are unknown.
questions.level_3: Backups exist and are documented, with a defined but untested recovery process.
questions.level_5: Recovery time and recovery point objectives are defined, tested regularly, and consistently met.

questions.question: Do you have a documented data owner for each critical dataset?
questions.level_1: No ownership is defined anywhere.
questions.level_3: Ownership defined for most datasets, documented in a data catalogue.
questions.level_5: All datasets have owners. Ownership triggers automatic quality alerts and SLAs.

questions.question: How do you know when your data is inaccurate, incomplete, or inconsistent?
questions.level_1: You find out when a report looks wrong or a client complains.
questions.level_3: Quality checks exist for key datasets, run on a defined schedule.
questions.level_5: Quality rules run continuously with automated alerts, and failures trigger a defined remediation process.

questions.question: If a number in a report looks wrong, can you trace it back to its source?
questions.level_1: No. Tracing a number back to its origin is manual guesswork, if it is possible at all.
questions.level_3: Lineage is documented for the most important reports and datasets.
questions.level_5: Lineage is tracked automatically end to end, from source system to final report, for all critical data.

questions.question: Do different teams use the same definition for shared reference data (customer, product, region)?
questions.level_1: Each team maintains its own version. Definitions conflict and nobody reconciles them.
questions.level_3: Core reference data is defined centrally, though some teams still maintain local variants.
questions.level_5: A single, governed source of reference data is used organisation-wide, with change managed through a formal process.

questions.question: Is there a data governance policy, and is it actually followed?
questions.level_1: No policy exists, or one exists but nobody references it.
questions.level_3: A policy exists, is documented, and is followed for the highest-risk data.
questions.level_5: The policy is enforced through tooling and monitoring, with compliance reviewed and reported regularly.

questions.question: If you asked three teams to define 'revenue' or your equivalent core metric, would you get the same answer?
questions.level_1: No. Each team calculates it differently and nobody has reconciled the difference.
questions.level_3: Core metrics are defined centrally and documented, though some legacy reports still diverge.
questions.level_5: A single certified metric layer feeds every report and dashboard. Divergence is not possible without approval.

questions.question: When someone needs a new report or analysis, what happens?
questions.level_1: They wait for IT or a data specialist to build it for them, however long that takes.
questions.level_3: Self-service BI tools exist and are used by trained staff for common questions.
questions.level_5: Self-service is the default across the business, with governance guardrails built into the tooling itself.

questions.question: Are the dashboards your organisation has built actually used?
questions.level_1: Dashboards exist but sit unopened. Decisions are made without them.
questions.level_3: Key dashboards are checked regularly by the teams they were built for.
questions.level_5: Dashboards are embedded in daily operating rhythm and decisions reference them directly, with usage itself monitored.

questions.question: How are your regular reports (weekly, monthly, board-level) produced?
questions.level_1: Manually, by someone assembling numbers from multiple sources by hand each time.
questions.level_3: Reports are templated and partially automated, with manual review before distribution.
questions.level_5: Reports generate automatically on schedule, from governed data, with exceptions flagged rather than manually checked.

questions.question: Can your analysts explore data freely to answer a new question, or only run pre-built reports?
questions.level_1: Only pre-built reports exist. Any new question requires a new request to IT.
questions.level_3: Analysts can query governed datasets directly for ad hoc analysis.
questions.level_5: Ad hoc exploration is standard practice, supported by a governed semantic layer that prevents inconsistent answers.

questions.question: Does your organisation have an environment where staff can experiment with models before committing to build one?
questions.level_1: No. There is no separation between experimentation and production, so nobody experiments.
questions.level_3: A defined experimentation environment exists, used by a small technical team.
questions.level_5: A managed experimentation platform is available broadly, with reusable tooling and tracked results.

questions.question: When a model is built, how does it reach production use?
questions.level_1: It does not. Models stay in notebooks or spreadsheets and are never deployed.
questions.level_3: A defined but manual deployment process exists, owned by a specific person or team.
questions.level_5: Models deploy through an automated, tested pipeline, consistent with how software is shipped elsewhere in the organisation.

questions.question: Once a model is live, how do you know if its performance has degraded?
questions.level_1: You do not monitor it. Degradation is discovered when outcomes visibly go wrong.
questions.level_3: Performance is checked periodically against a defined schedule.
questions.level_5: Performance and drift are monitored continuously, with automated alerts and a defined retraining trigger.

questions.question: Is data prepared and curated in a form that is ready for model-building, or does every project start from raw data?
questions.level_1: Every project starts from raw, unlabelled, uncurated data with no reuse between projects.
questions.level_3: Common features and datasets are documented and reused across projects.
questions.level_5: A governed feature store or equivalent makes curated, reusable data available to any project on demand.

questions.question: How does your organisation decide which AI or ML opportunities to pursue?
questions.level_1: There is no process. Ideas are pursued based on whoever is most enthusiastic at the time.
questions.level_3: A defined intake process exists, with opportunities assessed against feasibility and value.
questions.level_5: AI opportunities are prioritised through a structured, business-case-driven pipeline, reviewed and adjusted regularly.

questions.question: Does your senior leadership actively sponsor and invest in the data function?
questions.level_1: No. Data is treated as a cost centre with no executive champion.
questions.level_3: A senior sponsor exists and data initiatives receive defined, if limited, investment.
questions.level_5: Data strategy is set and actively championed at C-suite level, with investment tied to business outcomes.

questions.question: Do staff outside the data team have the skills to work confidently with data?
questions.level_1: No training exists. Data literacy varies entirely by individual initiative.
questions.level_3: Training is available and taken up by some teams, with basic literacy expected in relevant roles.
questions.level_5: A structured, organisation-wide data literacy programme is embedded, with literacy tracked as a workforce capability.

questions.question: Are data roles and responsibilities clearly defined across the organisation?
questions.level_1: No dedicated data roles exist. Data work is whatever falls to whoever is available.
questions.level_3: Core roles (owners, stewards, analysts, engineers) are defined for priority areas.
questions.level_5: A clear RACI for data roles exists organisation-wide and is reviewed as the organisation and its data needs evolve.

questions.question: How does the data team work with the rest of the business?
questions.level_1: The data team is siloed. Business units submit requests and wait, with little collaboration.
questions.level_3: Data specialists are aligned to business units and consulted on relevant projects.
questions.level_5: Data expertise is embedded within business units, shaping decisions from the start rather than reporting after the fact.

questions.question: When a significant decision is made, is data part of how it gets justified?
questions.level_1: Decisions are made on judgement and experience alone. Data is rarely consulted.
questions.level_3: Data is consulted for major decisions, though not consistently required.
questions.level_5: Data-driven justification is the expected standard for significant decisions, and this expectation is actively reinforced by leadership.
